title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned The Timekeeper's Lap Chart. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll.

options.label: The Timekeeper's Lap Chart
options.lineage: 1950s–70s circuit timekeepers' lap charts and stopwatch benches
options.thesis: The season kept the way a timekeeper kept it: ruled sheets, tabular ink, one column per lap, team colours as the ink each car is written in.
materials: ruled timing sheet on a dark bench
stopwatch bezel and red sweep hand
options.viewport: A pale ruled sheet on a dark bench fills the first viewport. Its header stamp: round, circuit, date, freshness. The body is the real lap chart of the last Grand Prix: one column per lap, one row per position, car numbers inked in team colour, the leader's line traced in red. A stopwatch scrubber under the sheet drags the whole chart lap by lap; standings sit as a billing block beside it, leader largest.
options.risk: Paper turns to kitsch the moment textures, stains or torn edges appear; the world is grid, ink and rules only. Typewriter numerals must hold at 12px or the density fails.

raised.raise: One strict monospaced grid governs every timing figure: all numerals tabular, all columns aligned across every sheet.
One scrubbable timeline binds the lap chart, the replay and the gap chart to the same lap cursor, deep-linkable by lap.
Standings carry hierarchy by size alone: the leader's name is set largest, the tail packed dense, no bars needed to read who matters.
Every weekend is a fixed station rail, FP1 → FP2 → FP3 → Q → Sprint → Race, and the sheet you are on is always stamped with its station.
Every card is ruled by the same header grid: title, round, station, date stamp, in the same positions on every sheet.

options.label: The Timing Tower
options.lineage: FIA live-timing screens and the broadcast timing tower
options.thesis: The dashboard as the pit wall's own timing screen: a full-height tower of 22 drivers, sector colours doing the talking.
options.viewport: A full-height timing tower on the left: position, team stripe, three-letter tag, gap, three sector mini-bars per driver, all in tabular mono. The right two-thirds holds the selected driver's sheet: lap chart, stints, speed trace.
options.risk: This is where most F1 dashboards land, including the current one; familiar and effective, but a reviewer may have seen it before.

options.label: Elbow Panel Console
options.thesis: Every tab is a colour bank inside one sweeping elbow frame; every control is a flat pill, every number a code cluster.
materials: flat pastel pills on pure black
elbow frames as the layout grid
options.viewport: A lilac elbow sweeps down the left and along the top; the Overview bank sits inside it as ranked pill segments: leader, last winner, next race, each a pill with its numeric cluster.
options.case: Fuses cleanly as an interface grammar with instant state changes and clear tab banks; loses on identification, this is a sci-fi bridge, not a paddock.
options.risk: Reads as pastiche of a specific television franchise the moment the elbows are recognisable.

options.label: ASCII Live Scene
options.thesis: Track maps and traces rendered as phosphor glyph density.
options.viewport: The replay as a glyph field, cars as at-signs.
options.case: Fuses poorly: glyph density cannot carry 22 team colours or sector times, and fans do not identify with terminal art.
options.kept: One strict monospace grid as the entire composition.

options.label: Cyclorama Dawn
options.thesis: Race weekend as light phases on an infinite horizon.
options.viewport: Horizon bands stacked from night to day, one per session.
options.case: Fuses poorly: gradient bands fight team colours, and horizon phases say nothing a fan recognises.
options.kept: A scrubbable cue timeline binding every view to one time cursor.

options.label: Festival Lineup Sheet
options.thesis: Standings as billing: size alone says who matters.
materials: one condensed face at eight sizes
options.viewport: Antonelli spans the width; the tail justified at the foot.
options.case: Carries the standings beautifully and nothing else; telemetry, sectors and replays have no place on a type-only sheet.
options.kept: Hierarchy by size alone; no bars where names suffice.

options.label: Darkroom Safelight
options.thesis: Results emerging slowly under amber light.
options.viewport: Each station a tray; the race develops in the last one.
options.case: Fuses poorly: an amber wash erases team identity, and fans want results instantly, not slowly.
options.kept: Work moves through fixed stations in order.

options.label: Sneaker Archive Wall
options.lineage: stacked sneaker boxes with end labels
options.thesis: Every round a box on the wall; pull one to open it.
options.viewport: A wall of 23 box ends, one per round.
options.case: Fuses poorly: a box per round hides the season's continuity that standings and lap charts depend on.
options.kept: One label grid ruling every card in the same positions.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: The broadcast-graphics dashboard every F1 site ships: dark ground, red accent, cards and bars, executed impeccably.
canonCard.viewport: Hero leader card, podium row, stat tiles, two standings columns.
canonCard.risk: Indistinguishable from the incumbent and from every other F1 dashboard by design.
